title: In nine great-ape populations, human regulatory DNA without mammal conservation does not lose more diversity where populations are larger; at most 5% of its bases have selection near s = 2.5e-5
abstract:
In great apes, human regulatory DNA that mammals do not conserve loses the same small fraction (1-5%) of its expected genetic variation in large and small populations. This matters because a recent claim says that this DNA is under weak natural selection that the small human population cannot show; that claim predicts a larger loss in larger populations, and we do not find it for the class as a whole or for its transposon-derived majority.

We used 72 great apes in 9 populations and 9 humans, genotyped with one pipeline on the human reference (Great Ape Genome Project). Background diversity, which is proportional to effective population size (Ne), differs up to 2.4-fold inside genera. We tested 62.8 million sites in 410,716 ENCODE candidate regulatory elements at least 2 kb from exons, with no base conserved across 241 mammals and no overlap with phastCons elements; 76% of the sites are in transposon-derived elements. The diversity deficit D is the fraction of expected diversity that is missing (0 for neutral DNA); expectations come from background DNA matched for three-base context, GC content, transposon status, distance to exons and to conserved DNA, and region.

Inside genera, D did not increase with background diversity: slope +0.002 per +0.001 diversity (bootstrap 95% CI -0.006 to +0.009) for the whole class and -0.002 (-0.010 to +0.006) for its transposon-derived part, against +0.048 predicted by a model fitted in wild mice (20% of bases with selection coefficient s = 2.5e-5). At most 5% of the bases can carry s = 2.5e-5, and at most 5-20% over the range of s that apes can show (5e-6 to 2e-4). Mammal-conserved non-coding DNA (+0.045) and amino-acid-changing coding sites (+0.041) showed the increase; random background and DNA beside the elements did not. Elements with little transposon DNA gave positive slopes (+0.017 to +0.019) that did not survive correction for 18 subgroups. GC-rich transposon-free elements gave +0.041, close to the mouse-model prediction, but this is unresolved because GC-rich background DNA moved strongly in the opposite direction and our context model does not fit GC-rich DNA.

Limits: elements are defined in human cells; the model assumes equilibrium and equal activity across genera; selection weaker than about 5e-6, or complete in every population, is not tested. Three independent reviews changed the analysis; earlier versions are included.

display.caption: Diversity deficit D (fraction of expected diversity that is missing) against background diversity for 9 great-ape populations and 2 human groups. A: elements with no mammal-conserved base that are mostly transposon copies (76% of sites); B: far elements with no conserved base and no transposon base (10%); C: mammal-conserved non-coding DNA. Bars: 95% block-bootstrap CIs. Dashed: the weak-selection model fitted in wild mice (20% of bases, s = 2.5e-5), started at the lowest-diversity taxon of each genus. D rises with diversity inside genera in C, not in A; B is unclear.

Difference in D between the higher- and lower-diversity population of each genus, by class of DNA (95% CIs). Black ticks: prediction of the mouse-fitted model for the non-conserved classes. Conserved non-coding DNA and 0-fold coding sites (positive controls) increase in chimpanzees and orangutans (in gorillas the 0-fold increase is small); non-conserved and transposon-derived elements do not; the GC-rich background control is noisy.

Largest fraction f of bases with selection coefficient s that agrees with the ape data (95%, profile at fixed s, one offset per genus, overdispersion-scaled, interpolated). Grey band: 4·Ne·s between 1 and 10 in the ape populations. Star and box: the model fitted in wild mice and its CI. The whole class and its transposon-derived part exclude the mouse best fit and nearly all of its CI.
